concepts.name: Geographical Distribution of Tea Cultivation in India
key_dimensions: Major producing states: Assam, West Bengal (Darjeeling), Tamil Nadu, Kerala — and the UPSC trap of distinguishing North India vs South India tea belts
Altitudinal and latitudinal variation: Darjeeling (high altitude, 600–2000m) vs Assam plains (50–100m) and their impact on quality
Emerging/non-traditional tea regions: Himachal Pradesh (Kangra), Uttarakhand, Sikkim, Tripura — often tested as exceptions
Comparison of share in production vs share in area: Assam dominates production (~55%) but Darjeeling commands premium pricing

concepts.name: Climatic and Soil Requirements of Tea
key_dimensions: Optimal conditions: temperature 20–30°C, rainfall 150–300 cm, well-distributed — trap: tea needs well-drained soil despite high rainfall demand
Soil type: Deep, fertile, well-drained loamy soil with acidic pH (4.5–5.5) — contrast with neutral pH crops
Frost sensitivity and the role of altitude in flavour (muscatel character in Darjeeling due to cool nights)
Why tea cannot grow in waterlogged conditions despite needing high rainfall — a classic UPSC conceptual trap

concepts.name: Types of Tea and Processing Methods
key_dimensions: Orthodox vs CTC (Crush, Tear, Curl) method — India's shift toward CTC for mass market, orthodox retained for export premium
Green tea, white tea, oolong, black tea — oxidation levels and India's production profile
Darjeeling GI tag: first Indian product to receive GI tag (2004) — frequently tested in GI/IPR context
Seasonal flushes: First flush (spring), Second flush (summer), Monsoon flush, Autumn flush — quality hierarchy

concepts.name: India's Tea Industry: Export Profile and Global Standing
key_dimensions: India as 2nd largest producer globally (after China) but NOT the largest exporter — Kenya, China export more
Major export destinations: Russia, UAE, UK, USA — shift away from traditional Soviet-era trade
Challenges to export competitiveness: rising wages, climate change impact on Assam yields, competition from Kenya/Sri Lanka
Darjeeling tea's GI protection in international markets and ongoing legal battles against misuse

concepts.name: Geographical Distribution of Coffee Cultivation in India
key_dimensions: India's coffee belt confined almost entirely to Southern Western Ghats: Karnataka (~70%), Kerala (~23%), Tamil Nadu (~5%) — UPSC trap: coffee is NOT pan-India unlike tea
Districts: Coorg (Kodagu), Chikmagalur, Hassan in Karnataka — most examined specific locations
Emerging regions: Andhra Pradesh (Araku Valley — tribal coffee, GI tagged), Odisha — non-traditional areas
Shade-grown coffee tradition in India vs sun-grown in Brazil — ecological and quality distinction

concepts.name: Varieties of Coffee Grown in India: Arabica vs Robusta
key_dimensions: Arabica: higher altitude (1000–1500m), better quality/flavour, lower yield, more disease-prone — grown in Chikmagalur, Nilgiris
Robusta: lower altitude, higher yield, stronger flavour, used in espresso blends — dominant in Kerala, parts of Karnataka
India's unique 'Monsooned Malabar' coffee — exposure to monsoon winds creates distinctive low-acid flavour, GI tagged
Trap: Robusta dominates India's production volume (~60%) but Arabica fetches higher price — reverse of common assumption

concepts.name: Climatic and Soil Requirements of Coffee
key_dimensions: Temperature: 15–28°C; sensitive to frost and extreme heat — restricts cultivation to specific elevation bands
Rainfall: 150–250 cm; needs dry spell during flowering (Oct–Nov) — trap: unlike tea, coffee needs a dry period
Soil: Well-drained, deep loamy soil rich in humus, slightly acidic — laterite and red soils of Western Ghats are ideal
Shade requirement: Coffee traditionally grown under shade trees (silver oak) — agroforestry model with biodiversity benefits

concepts.name: India's Coffee Export Profile and the Role of Coffee Board
key_dimensions: India exports ~70–80% of its coffee production — one of the most export-oriented plantation crops
Major destinations: Italy, Germany, Russia, Belgium — European dominance in Indian coffee exports
Coffee Board of India (statutory body under Ministry of Commerce): promotion, research, quality control — NOT under Agriculture Ministry, a common trap
Post-2000 liberalization: removal of pooling system allowed direct farmer-to-buyer sales, changing market dynamics

concepts.name: Geographical Distribution of Rubber Cultivation in India
key_dimensions: Kerala accounts for ~80% of India's natural rubber production — extreme concentration, a defining feature
Other states: Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Tripura, Goa — Tripura is the largest NE producer and fastest growing rubber state
Trap: Rubber cultivation is expanding to non-traditional areas (Assam, Meghalaya, West Bengal) due to climate shifts and policy push
District-level hotspots: Kottayam, Ernakulam, Thiruvananthapuram in Kerala

concepts.name: Climatic and Soil Requirements of Rubber (Hevea brasiliensis)
key_dimensions: Equatorial/tropical climate: temperature 25–35°C, rainfall 200–300 cm, uniform distribution — no dry season ideal
Altitude restriction: grows best below 600m — unlike tea and coffee which have altitude advantages
Soil: Deep, well-drained, laterite soil; tolerates slightly acidic conditions — similar to coffee but different from tea's need for higher acidity
Trap: Rubber is NOT native to India — introduced from Brazil via British (seeds smuggled from Amazon, grown in Kew Gardens)

concepts.name: Natural Rubber vs Synthetic Rubber: India's Production and Policy Context
key_dimensions: India is 4th largest natural rubber producer globally (after Thailand, Indonesia, Vietnam) — position often confused in exams
India is also one of the largest consumers — automotive sector (tyres) drives demand, making India a net importer despite large production
Import duty policy on rubber: a persistent tension between farmers (want high duty) and automobile industry (want low duty)
Rubber Board of India (statutory body) under Ministry of Commerce — parallel to Tea Board and Coffee Board, all under Commerce not Agriculture

concepts.name: Plantation Crops and the Three Statutory Boards: Tea Board, Coffee Board, Rubber Board
key_dimensions: All three boards are under Ministry of Commerce and Industry — UPSC frequently tests the ministry association as a trap
Functions: research, development, export promotion, quality certification, financial assistance to growers
Spices Board (for cardamom, pepper etc.) also under Commerce — contrast with Agriculture Ministry bodies like ICAR
Distinction: These boards regulate commodity-specific plantation crops under specific Acts (Tea Act 1953, Coffee Act 1942, Rubber Act 1947)

concepts.name: Plantation Agriculture: Structural and Colonial Legacy
key_dimensions: Plantation crops introduced/expanded under British colonial economy for export — tea (1840s Assam), rubber (early 1900s Kerala)
Land ownership patterns: historically large estates; post-independence, small-holder dominance emerged especially in rubber and coffee
Plantation Labour Act 1951: special labour protections for plantation workers — welfare provisions (housing, education, healthcare) — distinct from Industrial labour law
Trap: Tea is still dominated by large estates (especially in Assam) while rubber in Kerala is predominantly smallholder — opposite structures

concepts.name: Impact of Climate Change on Plantation Crops in India
key_dimensions: Tea: erratic rainfall in Assam, declining first-flush quality in Darjeeling due to warming — empirical studies showing yield decline
Coffee: White stem borer and leaf rust incidence increasing with temperature rise in Western Ghats — Arabica more vulnerable than Robusta
Rubber: Changing rainfall patterns in Kerala; expansion into NE India as climate becomes more suitable there
UPSC angle: Vulnerability of GI-tagged products (Darjeeling tea, Monsooned Malabar coffee) to climate change — economic and cultural loss

concepts.name: Geographical Indications (GI) Tags for Plantation Crops
key_dimensions: Darjeeling Tea: India's FIRST GI tag (2004) — trap: often confused with first GI tag globally or first agricultural GI
Munnar Tea, Nilgiri Tea, Assam Tea — other tea GIs with less prominence
Coorg Arabica Coffee, Chikmagalur Arabica Coffee, Araku Valley Arabica Coffee, Monsooned Malabar Coffee — multiple coffee GIs
GI Act 1999 and its administration by CGPDTM under Commerce Ministry — enforcement challenges in international markets

concepts.name: Intercropping, Agroforestry, and Sustainability Practices in Plantation Crops
key_dimensions: Coffee-pepper intercropping in Karnataka/Kerala — economic diversification for small farmers
Rubber-based agroforestry: banana, pineapple as intercrops in early years before canopy closure
Bird-friendly and shade-grown coffee certification: Western Ghats plantations as biodiversity hotspot corridors
Organic certification movement: Sikkim tea, tribal Araku coffee — premium market access and sustainable livelihoods link

concepts.name: Labour Issues and Social Dimensions of Tea Plantation Economy
key_dimensions: Tea garden workers in Assam/West Bengal: largely tribal/Adivasi communities brought by British — socioeconomic vulnerability
Closed tea gardens problem: ~60+ gardens closed in last decade due to economic unviability — displacement, starvation deaths reported
Child labour, gender wage gap, lack of land rights — persistent issues despite Plantation Labour Act 1951
UPSC GS2 link: Tea garden communities and their exclusion from forest rights, PESA applicability debates

concepts.name: Price Volatility and Market Mechanisms for Plantation Crops
key_dimensions: Tea auctions: Guwahati (largest in Asia for CTC tea), Kolkata, Cochin, Coimbatore, Siliguri — auction system vs direct sales
Rubber price collapse (2012–2020): impact on Kerala farmer suicides and migration — policy response through Rubber Price Stabilisation Fund
Coffee: International Coffee Agreement breakdown (1989) led to price crash — India's market exposure to global commodity cycles
MSP for plantation crops: Unlike food grains, NO statutory MSP for tea/coffee/rubber — a significant policy gap and UPSC trap

concepts.name: Comparison of Tea, Coffee, and Rubber: Cultivation Characteristics at a Glance
key_dimensions: Altitude preference: Tea (50–2000m, wide range), Coffee (600–1500m, mid-altitude), Rubber (below 600m, lowland) — clear hierarchy
Rainfall needs: Rubber > Tea > Coffee (Coffee uniquely needs dry spell for flowering)
Geographic concentration: Rubber most concentrated (Kerala 80%), Coffee moderately concentrated (Southern states), Tea more distributed (NE + South)
Export orientation: Coffee most export-oriented (~75%), Tea moderate (~20%), Rubber — India is net importer despite large production

concepts.name: North-East India's Role in Plantation Crops: Emerging Trends
key_dimensions: Assam: dominant in tea (~55% production), but infrastructure and labour challenges limit diversification
Tripura: 2nd largest rubber producer in India, fastest growing — government-promoted tribal rubber cultivation under TRDC
Meghalaya, Nagaland: emerging organic tea and coffee experiments — Act East Policy linkage for export to Southeast Asia
UPSC trap: Rubber in NE India is NOT Kerala-model large estate; it is predominantly smallholder tribal farming — structural difference
